core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Plantar Fasciitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes first-line stretching and activity modification, reserving imaging and injection for atypical or refractory cases, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excruciating sharp heel pain on the very first steps out of bed in the morning that improves gradually after walking around

Key HPI features: 52M standing retail worker presenting with a 3-month history of sharp heel pain, worst with the first steps out of bed in the morning, improving somewhat with walking but recurring after prolonged standing.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Point tenderness over the medial calcaneal tubercle, reproduced by passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass test). Tight Achilles tendon/gastrocnemius-soleus complex with reduced ankle dorsiflexion. No swelling, warmth, or bruising. Neurovascular exam intact, no plantar heel numbness. Able to bear weight fully.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Plantar Fasciitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Calcaneal stress fracture without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Inability to bear weight.
management_principles: Diagnosis is clinical, based on classic morning heel pain and point tenderness over the medial calcaneal tubercle; imaging is reserved for atypical cases or failure to improve
First-line treatment is stretching (plantar fascia and Achilles/calf), activity modification, and supportive footwear or heel cups, continued for 6-8 weeks before escalation
Consider a night splint or orthotics for persistent symptoms; reserve corticosteroid injection for refractory cases given the risk of fat pad atrophy or fascia rupture
Rule out calcaneal stress fracture or tarsal tunnel syndrome if pain is atypical, worsens with rest, or is accompanied by numbness.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 52M standing retail worker presenting with a 3-month history of sharp heel pain, worst with the first steps out of bed in the morning, improving somewhat with walking but recurring after prolonged standing.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Point tenderness over the medial calcaneal tubercle, reproduced by passive dorsiflexion of the toes (windlass test). Tight Achilles tendon/gastrocnemius-soleus complex with reduced ankle dorsiflexion. No swelling, warmth, or bruising. Neurovascular exam intact, no plantar heel numbness. Able to bear weight fully.
reference_soap.assessment: Plantar fasciitis, a clinical diagnosis based on the classic history and point tenderness over the medial calcaneal tubercle.
reference_soap.plan: Initiate first-line conservative treatment: daily plantar fascia and Achilles/calf stretching, ice/frozen water bottle rolling, supportive footwear or heel cups, and activity modification. Consider a night splint or orthotics if symptoms persist beyond 4-6 weeks. Reserve imaging for atypical presentations or failure to improve after 6-8 weeks, and reserve corticosteroid injection for refractory cases given the risk of fat pad atrophy or fascia rupture.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Plantar Fasciitis Heel Pain
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for excruciating sharp heel pain on the very first steps out of bed in the morning that improves gradually after walking around
Determine when imaging is warranted to rule out calcaneal stress fracture versus a straightforward clinical diagnosis of plantar fasciitis

teaching.one_liner: Degenerative microtearing of the plantar fascia causing intense heel pain on taking the first steps in the morning.

must_ask.say: Is the pain sharpest during the very first steps out of bed in the morning?
Does the pain ease off slightly as you walk around, but return after standing?
Is the pain located directly under the bottom inner side of your heel bone?
Have you recently increased running distance or changed to flat non-supportive shoes?
Do your calf muscles or back of ankle feel tight when stretching?
